System metadata rows are highlighted in the table and labeled **System Preset — Read Only**. You cannot edit or delete them, but you can see them when assigning metadata to documents.

## Applying metadata to documents

Metadata is assigned from the **Documents** page:

1. Select one or more documents.
2. Click the **Metadata** button.
3. The **Manage Metadata** dialog shows four sections:
   - **On All Documents** — metadata currently shared by every selected document.
   - **On Some Documents** — metadata that applies to only a subset of the selection, with a count such as `(2/3)`.
   - **Marked for Removal** — metadata that will be removed when you save.
   - **Available to Add** — metadata not currently on any selected document.

Click an item to move it between sections; click the **X** on a common item to mark it for removal. Click **Save Changes** to apply the result to all selected documents.

A document can have **many metadata entries** at once, and the same metadata value can be shared across many documents.

## Where metadata is used

Metadata key/value pairs are included when architxt pushes a document to a Hindsight memory bank. Hindsight receives them as the retain-time `metadata` object, so they become searchable, filterable context for every memory extracted from that document.

For details on how the metadata object is structured and consumed, see the Hindsight API documentation on [retain metadata parameters](https://hindsight.vectorize.io/developer/api/retain#metadata).

## How metadata fits into architxt

```text
        Metadata
            │
            ▼
       Documents  ──────►  Hindsight Memory Bank
            │
            ▼
   Contextual Graph / Mental Models / Reflect
```

Metadata is not part of the document text, but it rides along with the document. Used consistently, it becomes a powerful way to slice the corpus by source, author, domain, date, or any other dimension you define.

## Summary

Metadata is a flexible key/value layer for documents. Create your own pairs, import them in bulk, apply them to many documents, and architxt forwards them to Hindsight as part of every retain request.
---

# Tags
URL: https://architxtlabs.com/core-concepts/tags
# Tags

Tags in architxt are simple badge-style labels you attach to documents. They work like lightweight categories: `Project-Alpha`, `Billing-Module`, `Draft`, or `Reviewed`. Tags help you group documents in the UI, scope mental models, and drive Hindsight retention through both [`tags`](https://hindsight.vectorize.io/developer/api/retain#tags-and-document_tags) and [`document_tags`](https://hindsight.vectorize.io/developer/api/retain#tags-and-document_tags).

A document can have **many tags** at once. Tags are managed on the **Tags** page and applied from the **Documents** page.

## Creating and managing tags

Open the **Tags** page from the main navigation. The page lists every tag with its **Tag ID**, **Name**, **Documents** count, **Generated By** source, and creation time.

You can:

- Click **Add** to create a tag. Only a name is required.
- Click **Import** to paste a CSV of tag names. The optional header is `tag_name`; one tag per row.
- Select one or more tags and click **Delete**. Deleting a tag removes it from any documents that use it; the documents themselves stay in architxt.
- Search by name or generated-by source.

Click a tag row to open **Tag Details**. From there you can edit the name. If the tag is assigned to any documents that have already been synced to Hindsight, the dialog warns you that renaming it may cause a mismatch on the next sync.

## Applying tags to documents

Tags are assigned from the **Documents** page:

1. Select one or more documents.
2. Click the **Tags** button.
3. The **Manage Tags** dialog shows:
   - **On All Documents** — tags currently shared by every selected document.
   - **On Some Documents** — tags that apply to only a subset.
   - **Marked for Removal** — tags that will be removed when you save.
   - **Available to Add** — tags not currently on any selected document.

Click a tag to add it, click it again to remove it, and click **Save Changes** to apply the result to all selected documents. A document can have **many tags** at the same time.

You can also assign tags at upload time. In the **Upload** dialog, choose tags from the shared batch settings and every uploaded document will receive them automatically.

## Where tags are used

Tags serve two roles in Hindsight:

- They are included in the retain payload as [`document_tags`](https://hindsight.vectorize.io/developer/api/retain#tags-and-document_tags), so every memory extracted from the document carries those labels.
- Hindsight can also use tags for [tagging memories](https://hindsight.vectorize.io/developer/retain#tagging-memories) directly, making them a first-class filter and organization mechanism in the memory bank.

In architxt, tags are also used to scope **Mental Models**. A mental model's **Tags Match** setting controls which documents feed the model based on their tags.

## How tags fit into architxt

```text
         Tags
          │
          ├──► Mental Models / Reflect
          │
          ▼
     Documents  ──────►  Hindsight Memory Bank
```

Tags sit above individual documents. They are not part of the document text, but they travel with the document into Hindsight and influence which documents participate in mental models and Reflect workflows.

## Summary

Tags are quick, flexible labels for documents. Create them once, apply them to many documents, and they become part of both the architxt filtering model and the Hindsight memory-bank tagging model.
---

# Bank Settings
URL: https://architxtlabs.com/core-concepts/bank-settings
# Bank Settings

Bank Settings in architxt are a single master configuration that controls how content is retained, observed, and reflected inside Hindsight memory banks. Think of them as a template: edit them once in architxt, then push them to one or more Hindsight banks when you are ready to sync.

This page describes the settings you see in the **Bank Settings** UI and where each setting maps in the Hindsight API.

## The Bank Settings page

Open **Bank Settings** from the main navigation. The page shows one editable master configuration with three sections: **Missions**, **Extraction**, and **Disposition**.

Click **Edit** to change values, **Reset to defaults** to restore the built-in architxt defaults, or **Save** to store the master copy. Saving does **not** automatically push the settings to Hindsight — push happens from the **Hindsight** sync page.

### Missions

Missions are natural-language instructions that steer the model at different stages of the Hindsight pipeline.

| UI label | What it does | Hindsight reference |
|---|---|---|
| **Retain Mission** | Tells the model what facts to extract and how to structure them during retention. | [Steering extraction with a mission](https://hindsight.vectorize.io/developer/retain#steering-extraction-with-a-mission) |
| **Observations Mission** | Guides how raw facts are consolidated into higher-level observations. | [Observations mission](https://hindsight.vectorize.io/developer/observations#observations-mission), [`observations_mission`](https://hindsight.vectorize.io/developer/api/memory-banks#observations_mission) |
| **Reflect Mission** | Defines the persona and purpose used when answering Reflect queries. | [Mission natural language identity](https://hindsight.vectorize.io/developer/reflect#mission-natural-language-identity) |

### Extraction

Extraction settings control how Hindsight breaks up and processes source material.

| UI label | What it does | Hindsight reference |
|---|---|---|
| **Retain Extraction Mode** | Chooses the extraction strategy: `concise`, `verbose`, `custom`, `verbatim`, or `chunks`. | [`retain_extraction_mode`](https://hindsight.vectorize.io/developer/api/memory-banks#retain_extraction_mode) |
| **Retain Chunk Size** | Maximum chunk size, in tokens, used when splitting documents for retention. | [`retain_chunk_size`](https://hindsight.vectorize.io/developer/api/memory-banks#retain_chunk_size) |
| **Entities Allow Free Form** | When enabled, the model can create free-form entity labels instead of only using pre-defined architxt entities. | Part of the retain configuration sent to Hindsight |

### Disposition

Disposition sliders shape the tone of the Reflect persona. Each trait ranges from **1** to **5**.

| UI label | What it does | Hindsight reference |
|---|---|---|
| **Empathy** | How much the model mirrors the user's framing. | [Disposition traits](https://hindsight.vectorize.io/developer/reflect#disposition-traits) |
| **Literalism** | How strictly the model sticks to the source text. | [Disposition traits](https://hindsight.vectorize.io/developer/reflect#disposition-traits) |
| **Skepticism** | How willing the model is to challenge or qualify claims. | [Disposition traits](https://hindsight.vectorize.io/developer/reflect#disposition-traits) |

## Applying bank settings to a Hindsight bank

Bank Settings are not tied to a single bank until you sync them. From the **Hindsight** page:

1. Select a Hindsight server and bank.
2. Switch the object selector to **Bank Settings**.
3. Run **Diff** to compare architxt's master settings with the bank's current settings.
4. Click **Push** to overwrite the bank with the architxt master, or **Pull** to bring the bank's settings back into architxt.

The diff view shows per-field divergence badges for retain mission, observations mission, reflect mission, extraction mode, chunk size, free-form entities, and disposition.

## Where bank settings are used

Once pushed to a Hindsight memory bank, the settings become the bank's [`retain configuration`](https://hindsight.vectorize.io/developer/api/memory-banks#retain-configuration). They influence every subsequent retain, observation, and Reflect operation against that bank.

## How bank settings fit into architxt

```text
   architxt Bank Settings  (master)
            │
            ├──────── Push ────────►  Hindsight Memory Bank
            │                            │
            ▼                            ▼
       Documents / Mental Models  ►  Retain / Observe / Reflect
```

Bank Settings sit above individual documents and mental models. They define the global behavior applied when architxt pushes content to a Hindsight bank, and they can be pulled back from a bank to update the master configuration.

## Summary

Bank Settings are architxt's master Hindsight configuration. Edit missions, extraction mode, chunk size, and disposition locally, then push that configuration to any connected Hindsight memory bank to keep retention and reflection behavior consistent.
---

# Directives
URL: https://architxtlabs.com/core-concepts/directives
# Directives

Directives in architxt are hard rules you write to shape what the system remembers and how it answers. A directive is a short **Name** plus a **Statement** — for example, *“Always capture data flows as separate facts”* or *“Never invent entity aliases that are not in the source text.”* Directives can be active or inactive, have a priority, and can be tagged.

They map to Hindsight's [`directives`](https://hindsight.vectorize.io/developer/api/memory-banks#directives) concept and are enforced as [hard rules during Reflect](https://hindsight.vectorize.io/developer/reflect#directives-hard-rules).

## Creating and managing directives

Open the **Directives** page from the main navigation. The page lists every directive with **ID**, **Name**, **Statement**, **Active**, **Priority**, **Tags**, **Generated By**, and creation time.

You can:

- Click **Add** to create a directive. A **Name** and **Statement** are required; **Active** defaults to on and **Priority** defaults to `0`.
- Click **Import** to paste a CSV of directives. The optional header is `directive_name,directive_statement`; optional columns include `is_active` and `priority`.
- Select one or more directives and click **Delete** to remove them.
- Search by name, statement, generated-by source, priority, or tag.

Click a directive row to open **Directive Details** and edit its name, statement, active state, priority, and tags.

### Active vs inactive

Only **Active** directives are sent to Hindsight. Inactive directives stay in architxt but do not participate in retention or reflection. Use this to draft or temporarily disable a rule without losing it.

### Priority

Priority is a numeric ordering hint. Higher numbers sort earlier. Use it when two directives might conflict or when one rule should be considered before another.

### Tags

Directives can be tagged like documents and mental models. Tags are useful for grouping rules by domain, project, or severity. Select one or more directives and click **Tags** to add or remove tags in bulk.

## Where directives are used

Directives are pushed to Hindsight memory banks as part of the bank's [`directives`](https://hindsight.vectorize.io/developer/api/memory-banks#directives) configuration. Once there, they act as [hard rules for Reflect](https://hindsight.vectorize.io/developer/reflect#directives-hard-rules): the model must follow them when generating answers, and they influence how facts are extracted and observations are formed.

You sync directives from the **Hindsight** page, alongside documents, entities, mental models, and bank settings.

## How directives fit into architxt

```text
     Directives
          │
          ├──────────────►  Hindsight Memory Bank
          │                       │
          │                       ▼
          └──────────────►  Reflect / Retain
```

Directives are global rules. They do not belong to a single document, but they travel with the bank configuration and apply every time the bank retains content or answers a Reflect query.

## Summary

Directives let you write explicit rules that govern extraction and reflection. Keep them active, ordered by priority, and tagged so they reach the right Hindsight banks and shape answers the way you intend.
---

# AQL: architxt Query Language
URL: https://architxtlabs.com/core-concepts/aql
# AQL: architxt Query Language

AQL (architxt Query Language) is the compact, line-based language used to tell architxt which contextual data you want in a workspace section. It combines free-text intent with block directives, named outputs, and machine-readable entity or edge references.

AQL is used throughout the UI whenever you edit mental-model queries, focus a section, or compose a curated page.

## The basics

An AQL query is a plain text string. The parser recognizes three things:

1. **Intent text** — any plain sentence outside a block.
2. **Block directives** — `#graph`, `#table`, `#diagram`, or `#narrative` ... `#end`.
3. **References** — `[[Label (type:id)]]` for entities and `[[source — label → target]]` for edges.

Only one `#graph` block is allowed per query.

If you write only plain text, AQL treats it as an implicit narrative request:

```aql
What is the impact of the Order Engine on the Payment Gateway?
```

This is the simplest possible query: one intent, no blocks, no references.

## Block directives

Blocks define the shape of the answer. Each block starts with a `#` directive and ends with `#end`.

| Directive | Output shape |
|---|---|
| `#graph` | A contextual graph view of referenced entities and edges. |
| `#table` | One or more tables. |
| `#diagram` | A Mermaid diagram. |
| `#narrative` | Free-form prose. |

A block contains the prompt text the model should use inside that section.

### Graph block

```aql
#graph
Show how the Customer Registry and the Payment Gateway relate.
Customer Registry, Payment Gateway
#end
```

The body of the block is the content passed to the graph renderer.

### Narrative block

```aql
#narrative
Describe the integration flow between the Customer Registry and the Payment Gateway.
#end
```

### Table block

```aql
#table
#table-name Upstream dependencies
List every upstream service and the interface it uses.
#end
```

A `#table-name` sub-directive labels the table. Multiple `#table` blocks can appear in one query.

### Diagram block

```aql
#diagram
#diagram-name "Entity lifecycle"
#diagram-type sequenceDiagram
Alice->>Bob: Hello
#end
```

`#diagram-name` sets the title and `#diagram-type` selects the Mermaid renderer. Supported diagram types include:

- `flowchart`
- `sequenceDiagram`
- `classDiagram`
- `stateDiagram-v2`
- `erDiagram`
- `journey`
- `gantt`
- `pie`
- `timeline`
- `radar-beta`
- `architecture-beta`
- `mindmap`
- `venn-beta`

## Combining intent and blocks

Intent text written outside a block is preserved separately and used as the overall request.

```aql
compare current and desired state
#graph
Customer Registry
#end
```

The parser returns `intentText` = `compare current and desired state` plus a graph block with body `Customer Registry`.

You can also stack multiple blocks:

```aql
Summarize the architecture.
#narrative
#narrative-name Executive summary
Write a short paragraph for non-technical readers.
#end
#table
#table-name Components
List each component, its owner, and its status.
#end
```

## Sub-directives and scoping

Sub-directives only make sense inside specific block types. Using a sub-directive in the wrong block produces an error.

| Sub-directive | Allowed in | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `#graph-name` | `#graph` | Optional graph title. |
| `#narrative-name` | `#narrative` | Optional narrative title. |
| `#table-name` | `#table` | Optional table title. |
| `#diagram-name` | `#diagram` | Optional diagram title. |
| `#diagram-type` | `#diagram` | Required Mermaid diagram type. |

## Entity references with `[[...]]`

Entity references link an AQL query to actual entities in the contextual graph. The format is:

```aql
[[Label (type:id)]]
```

For example:

```aql
[[Order Engine (Component:COMP-002)]]
[[Payment Gateway]]
```

If the type is omitted, the parser treats the label itself as the ID:

```aql
[[Payment Gateway]]
```

This is useful for ad-hoc queries, but qualified references are preferred because they survive renames and disambiguate duplicate labels.

The UI provides a helper that builds these tokens for you:

```js
formatEntityToken('Order Engine', 'COMP-002', 'Component')
// => "[[Order Engine (Component:COMP-002)]]"
```

## Edge references

Edges use a longer form that names both endpoints and the relationship:

```aql
[[source — label → target]]
```

For example:

```aql
[[Order Engine — depends-on → Payment Gateway]]
```

The parser separates the string on em-dash (`—`) and arrow (`→`).

The UI helper is:

```js
formatEdgeToken('Order Engine', 'Payment Gateway', 'depends-on')
// => "[[Order Engine — depends-on → Payment Gateway]]"
```

## Stripping references

If you need the human-readable label without the markup, AQL can strip references back to plain text:

```aql
// Input
[[Order Engine (Component:COMP-002)]]

// Stripped
Order Engine
```

For edges, the strip keeps the readable path:

```aql
// Input
[[Order Engine — depends-on → Payment Gateway]]

// Stripped
Order Engine — depends-on → Payment Gateway
```

## Common errors

The parser validates AQL and returns error objects with a line number. Watch out for these mistakes:

| Query | Problem |
|---|---|
| `#graph\nCustomer Registry` | Unclosed block. Add `#end`. |
| `#graph\n#foo bar\n#end` | Unknown directive `foo`. |
| `#graph\n#table-name T\n#end` | `#table-name` is not allowed inside `#graph`. |
| `#end` | Unmatched `#end` with no opening directive. |
| `#diagram\n#diagram-type notARealDiagram\n#end` | Unknown diagram type. |

## Full example

A typical curated-page section query might look like this:

```aql
Explain the data flow from [[Order Engine (Component:COMP-002)]] to [[Payment Gateway (Component:COMP-015)]].
#diagram
#diagram-name "Data flow"
#diagram-type sequenceDiagram
OrderEngine->>PaymentGateway: invoice data
#end
#table
#table-name Interfaces
List each interface, its format, and owner.
#end
```

This produces:

- Intent text with two qualified entity references.
- A sequence diagram block named **Data flow**.
- A table block named **Interfaces**.

## Where AQL is used

- **Mental model form** — every mental model has an AQL query that defines its source data.
- **Workspace preview focus** — narrowing a previewed section generates AQL.
- **Curated page composition** — sections you add to a page carry AQL that can be re-edited later.
- **Reflect queries** — bespoke questions can be expressed as plain-text AQL intent.

## Summary

| Construct | Syntax | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Intent text | Plain sentence | Used as the overall request when no block is present. |
| Block | `#graph`, `#table`, `#diagram`, `#narrative` | Closed with `#end`. |
| Block name | `#graph-name`, `#table-name`, etc. | Optional title for the section. |
| Diagram type | `#diagram-type <type>` | Required inside `#diagram`. |
| Entity reference | `[[Label (type:id)]]` | Qualified references are preferred. |
| Edge reference | `[[src — label → target]]` | Separated by em-dash and arrow. |

AQL is intentionally small: a few directives plus two reference shapes. That small surface is enough to compose precise, grounded sections from the contextual graph.
---

# Overview
URL: https://architxtlabs.com/workspace/overview
# Overview

The **Workspace** is where you explore the contextual graph, run **Reflect** queries against a Hindsight memory bank, and assemble your findings into **curated pages**. It is designed as a persistent, multi-pane research surface: you select a server and bank, choose or create a session, and then move between querying, inspecting graph items, and composing pages.

## Primary UI areas

The Workspace page is divided into a top control bar, a left-hand work panel, a middle result/preview panel, and an optional right-hand **Chat** panel. Each area can be resized by dragging the handles between panes; double-click a handle to reset it. Use the **Data** and **Chat** toggles in the top bar to show or hide the left and right columns.

### Top bar

The top bar ties the Workspace to a specific Hindsight server and memory bank, and controls the active research session.

| Control | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **Server / Bank selectors** | Choose the Hindsight server and memory bank that feed the contextual graph and Reflect queries. |
| **Session selector** | Pick an existing research session or start a new one. Sessions are scoped to the selected server and bank. |
| **New / Edit / Delete session** | Create a new session, rename the active one, or delete it. Deleted sessions cannot be recovered. |
| **Data toggle** | Show or hide the left-hand data/query column. |
| **Chat toggle** | Show or hide the right-hand Chat panel. |

Sessions are the unit of persistence in the Workspace. A session remembers your Reflect history, curated pages, and the state of your tabbed views. The last active session for a given server/bank pair is restored automatically when you return.

### Left panel: scope, spine, and contextual data

The left column is split vertically into a **scope/query area** on top and a **bottom split** containing the **Entity spine** and **Contextual data** panes. You can hide the entire column with the **Data** toggle in the top bar.

| Pane | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **Scope / Reflect query** | Write and submit AQL-based Reflect queries. Toggle query options to adjust context and directives. |
| **Entity spine** | A filterable list of all grounded entities in the selected bank. It gives you a quick overview of what is in the graph, but is read-only here. |
| **Contextual data** | Shows entities that have attached mental models grouped under each entity. See [Contextual data](./contextual-data) for details. |

### Right panel: preview, curated pages, and chat

The right side is now split into a middle result/preview area and a dedicated **Chat** column. The result area shows either a read-only preview or an editable curated page, depending on the active tab. The Chat column is described in detail on the [Chat](./chat) page.

| Tab type | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **Preview** | The default anchor tab. Displays the result of a Reflect query, a selected step from the session history, or a mental-model content preview. |
| **View tabs** | Read-only tabs opened from the Contextual data panel, the Reflect history, or other preview actions. Each view tab isolates one result. See [Preview and curated pages](./preview-and-curated-pages) for details. |
| **Curated page tabs** | Editable pages where you compose narratives, tables, diagrams, and graphs from the session. Curated pages are saved inside the session. See [Preview and curated pages](./preview-and-curated-pages) for details. |
| **Chat threads** | Threaded agent conversations tied to the session. See [Chat](./chat) for details. |

Curated-page tabs show a dirty indicator when they have unsaved edits. You can save, rename, or delete the active curated page from the tab bar.

## Session management

A session is a container for a single research thread. When you create a session, it is empty: no queries, no pages, no view tabs, no chat threads. As you work, the session accumulates:

- Reflect query submissions and their results.
- Curated pages you create.
- View tabs you open from Contextual data or Reflect history.
- Chat threads and their message history.

Sessions are identified by an ID and a title. The title is optional; the UI falls back to the session ID and creation date. You can rename a session at any time.

:::tip[One session per server/bank pair]
Sessions are tied to a specific server and bank. Switching banks changes which sessions are available, but your open tabs and queries adapt to the new selection through the underlying research session hook.
:::

## Reflect workflow

1. Choose a server and bank.
2. Create or select a session.
3. Type an AQL query in the **Scope / Reflect query** pane and submit it, or type a question in the **Chat** panel.
4. The Reflect result appears in the **Preview** tab as an envelope (narrative, graph, tables, diagrams). The Chat result appears in the Chat column as a synthesized response with an envelope.
5. From either result, you can copy content into a curated page.
6. Curated pages are edited, saved, and managed as tabs in the middle panel.

## How it fits into architxt

```text
Contextual Graph / Hindsight  ──►  Workspace
                                        │
            ┌───────────────────────────┼───────────────────────────┐
            ▼                           ▼                           ▼
       Reflect queries            Contextual data                   Chat
       (questions to bank)        (attached mental models)          (agent Q&A)
            │                           │                           │
            └──────────►  Curated pages ◄───────────────────────────┘
                         (composed findings)
```

- **Context Patches** builds and maintains the graph and mental models that appear in the Workspace.
- **Reflect** provides the query engine and result envelopes.
- **Chat** adds a conversational layer with recall, synthesis, and merged edge-context graphs.
- **Workspace** gives you a persistent place to run queries, inspect model output, chat with the agent, and write pages.

## Summary

The Workspace is the user-facing research surface of architxt. Its top bar selects the data source and session and toggles the left data and right chat columns; its left panel provides querying and graph browsing; its middle panel previews results and hosts editable curated pages; and its right Chat panel lets you ask the agent about the bank.
---

# Chat
URL: https://architxtlabs.com/workspace/chat
# Chat

The **Chat** panel is the third column in the Workspace. It lets you have a focused, threaded conversation with the architxt agent about the entities, memories, and relationships in the active Hindsight bank. Each research session can contain multiple isolated chat threads, so you can keep separate conversations for different questions.

## Where it lives

The Chat panel sits to the right of the curated-page area in the Workspace. You can show or hide it with the **Chat** toggle in the top control bar, and you can resize it by dragging the handle between the page area and the chat column.

## Chat threads

A thread is an independent conversation inside a research session. The thread bar at the top of the chat column lists open threads and provides controls for managing them.

| Action | How to use it |
|---|---|
| **Create a thread** | Click the **+** button. New threads are named `Chat 1`, `Chat 2`, and so on. |
| **Switch threads** | Click a tab, or choose a thread from the dropdown. The dropdown also lists threads that have been closed but still exist. |
| **Rename a thread** | Click the pencil button and type a new name. |
| **Delete a thread** | Click the trash button. Deleting a thread removes all of its messages. |
| **Close other tabs** | Click the **X** button to close every thread tab except the active one. The threads themselves remain available from the dropdown. |

Threads are tied to the selected research session. Switching sessions switches to that session's set of threads.

## Sending a message

The chat input is a CodeMirror editor that behaves like a small text area with autocomplete:

Type a plain-language question about the bank, for example "What depends on the billing service?" or "Explain the customer onboarding flow."
- `[[` opens the entity/edge reference completer. Choose an entity to insert a canonical reference such as `[[Billing Service (Component:EXAMPLE-001)]]`.
- `##` opens the block-reference completer if the current chat turn produced an AQL query with named blocks.
- Press **Enter** to send.
- Press **Alt+Enter** or **Shift+Enter** to insert a new line without sending.

Messages are saved as you send them, so reloading the page or returning later restores the thread history.

## How the agent responds

When you send a message, the agent follows a deterministic pipeline:

1. **Entity resolution** — extracts any entity or edge references from your message and resolves them to canonical `type:entity_id` form.
2. **Recall from Hindsight** — when the session is backed by a Hindsight bank, the agent runs a recall query against world facts and observations, weighted toward the resolved entities.
3. **Synthesis** — a reasoning model summarizes the recalled memories as a concise IT-architect-style answer. The response is plain prose; inline source markers such as `[1]` or `【...】` are forbidden.
4. **Graph merge** — edge-context graphs for the resolved and synthesized entities are merged into a single graph you can inspect.
5. **Contextual items** — attached mental models for the same entities are collected and shown below the response.

The final reply is rendered as a unified envelope: narrative, graph, and contextual items in one place.

## Reading the response

| Part | What it shows |
|---|---|
| **Agent response card** | The synthesized answer, collapsed to a fixed height by default. Click **Show more** to expand it, or **Show less** to collapse it. |
| **Envelope viewer** | If the response has structured sections, the card renders the full `EnvelopeViewer` with the usual controls. Use **Add to page** to copy a section into the active curated page. |
| **Graph button / evidence icon** | Opens the merged edge-context graph. Evidence collected from the graph edges is available in the evidence modal. |
| **Contextual data card** | Lists mental models attached to the entities in the response: node summaries, capability models, discovery models, and edge-context models. Each item shows the entity name, model role, and title. |

The agent response card shows the model name and token count at the bottom when the reply came from the LLM synthesizer.

## Contextual data card

The card below an agent reply works like a compact version of the main Contextual data panel:

- **ALL / NODES / EDGES** toggles filter the list by scope.
- Type in the search box to filter by entity name, id, role, or model title. Searches are multi-word AND, so `ime charging` matches items that contain both words somewhere in their visible fields.
- Click an item to open its model in the current curated-page tab, or click the external-link icon to open it in a new tab.
- Items are deduplicated and sorted by role scope: entity summaries first, then capability models, discovery models, and edge-context models.

## How it fits into the Workspace

```text
Research session
        │
        ├── Reflect queries ──► Preview / results
        ├── Curated pages ──► Editable findings
        └── Chat threads ─────► Agent-driven Q&A with recall + graph
```

Chat reuses the same entity resolver, recall, and contextual-data paths as Reflect and the Contextual Graph Manager. The difference is that Chat wraps them in a conversational thread with synthesized answers and a merged evidence graph.

## Summary

- Chat is a third Workspace column with threaded conversations per session.
- Threads can be created, renamed, deleted, and reopened from the dropdown.
- The agent resolves entities, recalls memories, synthesizes an answer, and merges edge-context graphs.
- Replies render as unified envelopes with narrative, graph, evidence, and attached mental models.
- Use the response controls to add sections directly to a curated page.
---

# Contextual data
URL: https://architxtlabs.com/workspace/contextual-data
# Contextual data

The **Contextual data** panel in the Workspace brings every mental model related to an entity into one place. It does not distinguish between where a model lives in architxt — plain, derived, or contextual — it simply shows what is available for the selected entity and lets you open it.

## What the panel shows

The panel lists entities that have at least one attached mental model. Each row is an entity; expanding the row reveals the models attached to it. The same entity can appear because it has:

- A **plain** mental model stored directly on the entity in architxt.
- A **derived** mental model produced by a template role applied to the entity's catalog record.
- A **contextual** mental model generated from the contextual graph node.
- An **edge-context** model that explains relationships between this entity and others.

All of these are grouped under the entity's identity. The panel uses the entity name from the catalog or contextual graph, and shows the underlying entity ID in a monospace label so you can always see which object the models belong to.

## Model scope badges

Each attached model shows a scope badge that tells you how it is attached:

| Badge | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **PLAIN** | A plain mental model stored directly on the architxt entity. |
| **DERIVED** | A template-derived mental model from the entity's catalog record. |
| **NODE** | A contextual mental model generated for this graph node. |
| **EDGE** | An edge-context model describing a relationship to another entity. |
| **SEED** | A discovery/seed contextual model around this entity. |

The badge tells you how the model was produced; the role label next to it tells you what kind of model it is — for example, summary, capabilities, edge context, or a custom template role.

## Filtering and search

The panel header contains controls that help you find the right model quickly when the entity list is large.

| Control | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **ALL / NODES / EDGES** | Scope filter. **ALL** shows every attached model. **NODES** limits the list to entity-level models (plain, derived, and node/seed scopes). **EDGES** shows only edge-context models that describe a relationship. |
| **Search box** | Freetext filter across entity names, entity IDs, scope badges, role labels, and model titles. Typing multiple words performs an AND search, so `acme products` only keeps rows that contain both words somewhere in their visible fields. |
| **Counter** | Shows the total number of items in scope and how many match the current filter, for example `12 (4)`. |

The search applies to every item in the panel, including models inside collapsed entities. If an entity has no matching models under the current filter, it is hidden entirely.

## Deduplicated edge-context items

Edge-context models can be discovered from both endpoints of a relationship. The panel deduplicates these so a single edge appears only once, sorted with the alphabetically earlier endpoint first. This keeps the list compact and avoids mirror duplicates when both entities are in scope.

## Interaction model

| Action | What happens |
|---|---|
| **Click a model** | Opens the model content in the active **Preview** tab (or replaces the current view tab). |
| **Open in new tab** | Opens the model in a new read-only **View** tab, so you can keep the current tab open. |
| **Expand / collapse entity** | Shows or hides the attached models for that entity. |
| **Filter by scope or search** | Narrows the visible items without changing what is attached to each entity. |

## Why this matters

In other parts of architxt, mental models are managed in different places:

- **Plain and derived** models are created and edited on the main **Mental Models** page and in the Hindsight sync flows.
- **Contextual** models are produced automatically by the Context Patches sync job.
- **Edge-context** models are built from the relationships in the contextual graph.

The Contextual data panel is the only place where all of these are brought together under the entity they describe. This makes it the right surface for:

- Checking whether an entity has a summary before running a Reflect query.
- Comparing how the same entity is described by different model types.
- Opening a model in a new tab for side-by-side reading.
- Finding the edge context for a relationship you want to include in a curated page.

## Example

Consider an entity labeled **Acme Corp**.

| Model | Scope | Role | How you see it |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Acme Corp summary` | DERIVED | `sys_entity_summary` | From the catalog-derived models. |
| `Acme Corp capabilities` | NODE | `sys_entity_capabilities` | From the contextual graph node. |
| `Acme Corp → Products division` | EDGE | `sys_edge_context` | From a graph relationship. |
| `Acme Corp strategy` | PLAIN | Custom template role | Created directly in architxt. |

All four rows appear when you expand **Acme Corp** in the Contextual data panel, even though they came from different sources.

## Relationship to other surfaces

- **Context Patches → Mental Models tab** shows every contextual/role-based model for the bank at once. The Contextual data panel filters that same information to a single entity and mixes in plain and derived models. That tab now also supports scope filters (**All / Empty / Failed**) and search, which mirrors the filtering behavior in the Contextual data panel.
- **Mental Models (main page)** is where you create and edit plain and derived models; their content flows here.
- **Workspace → Preview / View tabs** is where you land when you click or open a model from this panel.
- **Workspace → Chat** reuses the same contextual-item list, scoped to the entities the agent resolved in a reply.
- **Curated pages** let you copy content from previewed models into a composed page.

## Summary

The Contextual data panel is the collation point for everything an entity knows. It gathers plain, derived, contextual, and edge-context models under one identity, lets you preview them in place or open them in a new tab, and connects directly to the rest of the Workspace for reading and composition.
---

# Reflect queries and session items
URL: https://architxtlabs.com/workspace/reflect-queries-and-session-items
# Reflect queries and session items

The Workspace is built around asking questions and keeping track of the answers. **Reflect queries** are how you ask Hindsight a question in natural language, and **session items** are the record of every question and its result in the current session.

## Reflect query panel

The **Scope / Reflect query** panel sits at the top of the left column. It is a single-purpose query surface: you type a question, adjust options if you need to, and submit it. The answer appears in the **Preview** tab as an envelope that can contain narratives, graphs, tables, and diagrams.

### Writing a query

Queries are plain text. The editor gives you autocomplete helpers:

- Type `#` to see base document section types.
- Type `[[` to see the list of grounded entities and edges from the contextual graph.

You can double-click an entity or edge in the autocomplete to insert it into the query. This is useful when you want the model to reason about a specific known entity rather than relying on the query text alone.

:::tip[AQL syntax errors]
Reflect now surfaces AQL syntax errors directly in the Run Query flow. If the query cannot be parsed, the Preview tab shows the error message and the query is not submitted.
:::

### Query options

Click the **Options** switch to show the Reflect-specific options. The defaults are sensible for most queries, but you can change them when you need tighter control.

| Option | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| **Fact types** | `world`, `observation` | Restricts the kinds of facts Reflect can draw on. |
| **Budget** | `high` | How much retrieval and generation effort to spend. Options are `low`, `mid`, `high`. |
| **Max tokens** | `4096` | Maximum length of the generated response. |
| **Include source facts** | Off | When on, the response includes the source facts used to generate it. |
| **Exclude mental models** | Off | When on, Reflect ignores plain and derived mental models attached to entities. |

### Submitting and status

Press the **Run Query** button or hit Enter to submit. While the query is running, the Preview tab shows a loading state and the session item row displays a running indicator. If the query fails, the error appears in the Preview tab and the session item shows a failed status.

## Session items panel

The **Session items** panel sits below the query panel in the left column. It lists every step in the current session, in chronological order. Each item represents one query or one curated page created in the session.

### Origin filter chips

The panel header contains filter chips that limit the visible session items by where they came from. Click a chip to toggle it. This makes it easier to find, for example, only Reflect results or only curated pages in a busy session.

### Searching session items

A freetext search filter in the panel header lets you narrow the list by title or query text. Multi-word searches use AND matching, so `charging singleview` shows only items that contain both words.

### What each item shows

| Element | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Timestamp** | When the item was created. |
| **Status dot** | `running`, `failed`, or completed. |
| **Title or query preview** | If the item has a title, the title is shown; otherwise the first line of the query is shown. |
| **Expand chevron** | Multi-line queries can be expanded to show the full text. |

### Panel counters

The session items header shows the total number of items in scope and how many match the active filters, for example `5 (2)`. This mirrors the counter style used elsewhere in the Workspace.

### Actions on an item

| Action | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Click the item** | Opens the result in the active Preview tab. |
| **Open in new tab** | Opens the result in a new read-only View tab. |
| **Edit title** | Gives the item a readable title so you can find it later. |
| **Re-use** | Copies the query text back into the Reflect query input so you can edit and resubmit it. |
| **Re-run** | Submits the same query again, producing a new result. |
| **Provenance** | Opens the query-inspection dialog to see the full request and response metadata. |
| **Delete** | Removes the item from the session permanently. |

### Item types in the list

Session items are not limited to Reflect queries. The same list also includes:

- **Reflect results** — the answers returned by Reflect.
- **Curated pages** — pages you created and saved inside the session.
- **Mental-model previews** — items opened from the Contextual data panel.

The title or preview text, the status dot, and the available actions adapt to the item type.

## Typical workflow

1. Type a Reflect query in the top-left panel.
2. Submit it and watch the result appear in the Preview tab.
3. The new item appears in the Session items list.
4. Optionally give the item a title so you can find it again.
5. Re-use, re-run, or open the item in a new tab as needed.
6. Copy content from the preview into a curated page.

## How it fits into the Workspace

```text
Reflect query  ──►  Preview  ──►  Curated page
     │
     ▼
Session items  ──►  Re-use / Re-run / Inspect
```

- The **Reflect query** panel is the input surface.
- The **Preview** tab shows the current output.
- **Session items** are the persistent history that let you return to, reuse, or compare earlier results.
- **Curated pages** are where selected results become part of a composed document.

## Summary

Reflect queries and session items are the question-and-answer loop of the Workspace. The query panel lets you ask Hindsight anything about the selected bank; the session items list keeps every question and answer in order so you can navigate, revisit, and build on your research.
---

# Preview and curated pages
URL: https://architxtlabs.com/workspace/preview-and-curated-pages
# Preview and curated pages

The middle of the Workspace is a tabbed surface split into two kinds of tabs: **Preview** tabs are read-only, and **curated page** tabs are editable. Both are scoped to the active research session, so what you open and save travels with the session. The Chat column on the far right also produces envelope-like responses that can be copied into curated pages.

## Preview tabs

A **Preview** tab shows the rendered output of a single Reflect result, a mental-model content preview, or any other envelope opened from the Workspace. It is read-only and exists to let you inspect a result before deciding whether to copy it into a curated page.

### What a preview can contain

A preview envelope may contain any combination of:

| Section | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **Narrative** | Prose blocks, headings, and lists answering the query. |
| **Diagram** | Mermaid diagrams rendered inline with copy/export controls. |
| **Table** | Tabular results with column headers and row data. |
| **Graph** | Entity/edge visualisations built from the contextual graph. |

Each envelope is independent. The preview tab shows whichever directive produced it, but you do not edit the envelope here.

### Preview controls

| Control | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Index** | Show or hide paragraph/section numbers for quick reference. |
| **Plain** | Strip formatting and view the raw text. |
| **Copy** | Copy the full envelope or a selected section to the clipboard. |
| **Save as Markdown** | Download the rendered content as a `.md` file. |
| **Render Markdown** | Toggle inline Markdown rendering for source blocks. Defaults to on. |

:::tip[Copy to a curated page]
From a preview or from a Chat agent response you can copy a section directly into an open curated page. This is the fastest way to move from a Reflect answer or chat result to a composed document.
:::

:::tip[Markdown spacing]
When a preview or chat response contains multiple envelope sections, the renderer inserts blank lines between sections so that headings and prose do not run together.
:::

## Curated pages

**Curated pages** are editable documents you build inside a session. A page is a sequence of sections; each section is a discrete block such as a narrative paragraph, a diagram, a table, or a graph. Sections can be reordered, edited, removed, and restored while the page remains unsaved.

### Creating and managing a page

| Action | How it works |
|---|---|
| **New page** | Create a blank curated page from the tab bar. You can pick a title or let the UI assign one based on the first content. |
| **Rename** | Double-click the tab title or use the tab menu. |
| **Save** | Save the page explicitly. Until you save, changes are held in memory and the tab shows a dirty indicator. |
| **Delete** | Remove the page from the session. This cannot be undone. |
| **Reorder tabs** | Drag curated-page tabs to change their order. |

### Curated-page sections

Sections are the building blocks of a curated page. The editor shows each section with its own controls.

| Section type | Editing notes |
|---|---|
| **Narrative** | Edit prose directly; headings, lists, and paragraphs are preserved. |
| **Diagram** | Edit the Mermaid source; the renderer updates as you type. |
| **Table** | Edit cells, add or remove rows and columns. |
| **Graph** | Graph sections are read-only snapshots from previews. |

### Soft delete and restore

When you remove a section, it is not immediately discarded. The editor keeps a soft-deleted section visible until you save the page, so you can restore it if you change your mind. Once the page is saved, deleted sections are removed permanently.

### Dirty state

A curated-page tab shows a dirty indicator as soon as you add, edit, delete, or reorder a section. Saving clears the indicator. If you close the tab with unsaved changes, the editor prompts you to save or discard.

## Evidence modal

When a preview or chat graph includes evidence, you can open the evidence modal to inspect the source documents and memories behind it.

| Control | Behavior |
|---|---|
| **Source documents** | Collapsed by default. Expand a document to see its metadata and the chunks that support the selected evidence. |
| **Chunk text** | The text of a chunk appears when you expand it. Selecting a document loads all of its chunks at once. |
| **Document metadata** | Document details appear when you expand a source document. |

## From preview or chat to curated page

The typical flow is:

1. Run a Reflect query, open a mental-model preview, or ask the Chat agent a question.
2. Inspect the result in a read-only Preview tab or in the Chat column.
3. Copy one or more sections from the preview or chat response.
4. Paste them into a curated page, or create a new page from the copied content.
5. Edit, reorder, and supplement the sections until the page says what you need.
6. Save the curated page to persist it in the session.

Agent responses in Chat also expose an **Add to page** action on each envelope section, so you can move a chat result into a curated page without switching tabs.

## How it fits into the Workspace

```text
Reflect query / Chat reply ──► Preview tab (read-only)
                                    │
                                    ▼
                         Curated page (editable, saved in session)
                                    │
                                    ▼
                      Contextual data / mental-model sources
```

- **Reflect queries** and **Chat replies** produce the content that lands in previews.
- **Preview tabs** let you inspect and select content.
- **Curated pages** let you compose the final document.
- **Session items** record the query, chat, and curated-page history for later review.

## Summary

Preview tabs are read-only windows onto Reflect results, Chat agent responses, and mental-model content. Curated pages are editable session-scoped documents made of sections that can be copied from previews or chat, edited, reordered, and saved.
---

# Focus: narrative
URL: https://architxtlabs.com/workspace/focus-narrative
# Focus: narrative

A **narrative** directive asks architxt to answer a question or explore a topic in plain prose. It is the most common output type in Reflect and the simplest to turn into a curated page.

## When to use a narrative focus

Use narrative when you want:

- A summary of entities, relationships, or documents.
- A walkthrough of a process or argument.
- An explanation in paragraphs with headings and lists.
- Content that is easy to edit, reorder, and save as Markdown.

## What a narrative envelope looks like

A narrative envelope is a document-style result. It is composed of sections that map directly to curated-page sections:

| Element | Typical content |
|---|---|
| **Title** | The question or topic the narrative answers. |
| **Headings** | Logical sections such as “Overview”, “Key entities”, “Implications”. |
| **Paragraphs** | Prose paragraphs that cite or describe the underlying data. |
| **Lists** | Bulleted or numbered lists for grouped facts. |

Narrative output is plain text first. Diagrams, tables, and graphs are produced by other directive focuses and can be combined with narrative on a curated page.

## Preview mode

In a Preview tab a narrative envelope is shown through the narrative viewer. The viewer renders headings, paragraphs, and lists and adds section-level controls.

| Control | Behavior |
|---|---|
| **Index** | Adds paragraph/section numbers for easy citation. |
| **Plain** | Strips formatting to show bare text. |
| **Copy** | Copies the whole narrative or an individual section. |
| **Save as Markdown** | Exports the rendered narrative as `.md`. |

Narrative previews have no diagram source tab or table grid because the content is already text.

## Curated-page editing

When you copy a narrative section into a curated page, it becomes an editable text section. You can:

- Edit the prose directly in the section editor.
- Split or merge paragraphs.
- Reorder sections relative to diagrams, tables, and graphs.
- Soft-delete and restore sections until you save.

:::tip[Edit with the envelope in mind]
A narrative section remembers its source envelope. If the underlying query or mental model changes, you may want to re-copy the section rather than editing it by hand.
:::

## Consistency tips

To get predictable narrative results:

- Be explicit in the query about tone and depth: “summarise in three paragraphs” or “list the five most important points”.
- Use directives to constrain the answer when the bank contains many entities.
- Break large questions into smaller queries and combine the answers on a curated page.

## Relationship to other pages

- [Directives](../core-concepts/directives) explains how directives shape Reflect output.
- [Mental models](../core-concepts/mental-models) describes the plain/derived/contextual model pipeline that feeds narratives.
- [Preview and curated pages](./preview-and-curated-pages) covers the broader tab model this focus type fits into.

## Summary

The narrative focus is prose-first output from Reflect. It renders as a structured document in the Preview tab and maps cleanly to editable sections in curated pages.
---

# Focus: diagram
URL: https://architxtlabs.com/workspace/focus-diagram
# Focus: diagram

A **diagram** directive asks architxt to explain a relationship, flow, or structure as a visual diagram. architxt renders diagrams as [Mermaid](https://mermaid.js.org/) flowcharts, so you can inspect, edit, copy, and export them like any other Mermaid source.

## When to use a diagram focus

Use a diagram focus when you want:

- A visual map of how entities connect.
- A flowchart of a process, decision tree, or lifecycle.
- A structure that is easier to understand as nodes and edges than as prose.
- Content you can drop straight into documentation or presentations.

## What a diagram envelope looks like

A diagram envelope contains one or more diagram blocks. Each block has:

| Field | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **Name** | The title shown above the rendered diagram. |
| **Type** | The diagram type, typically `flowchart` for Reflect output. |
| **Content** | Raw Mermaid source (without Markdown fence markers). |
| **Evidence** | Optional references to source data that informed the diagram. |

Diagram blocks are rendered inline in the Preview tab and in the curated-page editor.

### Preview controls

Diagram previews share the common envelope controls and add a few diagram-specific ones.

| Control | Behavior |
|---|---|
| **Copy** | Copies the Mermaid source, the rendered SVG, or a PNG image of the diagram. |
| **Fit** | Toggles fit-to-width so large diagrams shrink to the panel width. The modal opens with fit enabled. |
| **Zoom / Pan** | Floating controls let you zoom in, zoom out, and drag the diagram around. |
| **Focus** | Opens the diagram in a modal with the source visible and, when the source is editable, an **Apply** button. |

:::tip[Fit toggle style]
The Fit control is rendered as a slider+label and follows the same style as other toggle controls in the Workspace.
:::

:::tip[Copy formats]
From the diagram header you can copy the raw Mermaid source, copy the SVG, or copy a PNG image. This makes it easy to paste into Slack, Notion, GitHub, or another document.
:::

## Editing diagrams in curated pages

When you add a diagram to a curated page it becomes an editable diagram section. The section editor shows the Mermaid source on one side and a live preview on the other.

| Action | How it works |
|---|---|
| **Edit source** | Change the Mermaid text; the preview updates as you type. |
| **Rename** | Edit the diagram name in the modal or section header. |
| **Apply** | Save the edited source back to the curated page. |
| **Soft delete** | Remove the section; restore it before saving if you change your mind. |

:::tip[Syntax errors block apply]
The editor validates the Mermaid source and disables **Apply** while the diagram contains syntax errors. Fix the error first, then apply your changes.
:::

### Renderer override

Mermaid chooses the layout renderer from frontmatter in the diagram source. You can override the default renderer by adding a `config` block at the top of the source. See the [Mermaid configuration syntax reference](https://mermaid.ai/open-source/intro/syntax-reference.html#configuration) for full details.

```mermaid
---
config:
  layout: elk
---
flowchart TD
  A --> B
```

`dagre` is the default layout. `elk` can be useful for complex diagrams with many crossing edges, because it often produces a tidier layout. The renderer is part of the source, so it travels with the diagram when you copy or save it.

:::tip[Use frontmatter, not a control]
The Preview tab does not provide a renderer switch in its control panel. To use `elk`, edit the Mermaid source directly in the Focus modal or curated-page section editor and add the `config: layout: elk` frontmatter block.
:::

:::tip[Mermaid type detection]
Diagram sources that include a type directive after the frontmatter are detected automatically, and the Fit header is shown consistently regardless of how the type is declared.
:::

## From diagram to curated page

The typical flow is:

1. Ask a Reflect question that requests a diagram, or open a mental model whose output is a diagram.
2. Inspect the rendered Mermaid in the Preview tab.
3. Zoom, pan, or switch renderer until the layout is readable.
4. Copy the diagram (source, SVG, or PNG) or copy the section into a curated page.
5. In the curated page, refine the Mermaid source if needed, then save the page.

## Relationship to other focus pages

Diagrams often appear alongside narrative, table, and graph sections in the same envelope. A single Reflect result can contain a short narrative followed by a diagram that illustrates it. You can mix all of these section types on one curated page.

- [Focus: narrative](./focus-narrative) for prose sections.
- [Preview and curated pages](./preview-and-curated-pages) for the tab model this focus type fits into.

## Summary

The diagram focus turns Reflect output into Mermaid flowcharts. Previews give you copy, fit, zoom, and renderer controls; curated-page sections let you edit the source live and save the result.
---

# Focus: table
URL: https://architxtlabs.com/workspace/focus-table
# Focus: table

A **table** directive asks architxt to organise information into rows and columns. Tables are useful when you need a compact, scannable answer that compares entities, lists properties, or enumerates values. Like other focus types, a table can stand alone or be combined with narrative, diagram, and graph sections on a curated page.

## When to use a table focus

Use a table focus when you want:

- A side-by-side comparison of entities or concepts.
- A property grid: each entity as a row, each attribute as a column.
- A ranked or enumerated list with multiple fields per item.
- Output that is easy to paste into a spreadsheet or report.

## What a table envelope looks like

A table envelope contains one or more table blocks. Each block has:

| Field | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **Name** | The title shown above the table. |
| **Columns** | The column headers that define what each cell means. |
| **Rows** | The data values, one row per record or entity. |
| **Evidence** | Optional references to source data that informed the table. |

Table blocks are rendered as a scrollable grid in the Preview tab and in the curated-page editor.

## Preview controls

Table previews share the common envelope controls and add a few table-specific ones.

| Control | Behavior |
|---|---|
| **Copy** | Copies the table as CSV, Markdown, or a plain text grid. |
| **Search** | Filters rows by typing a substring match across all cells. |
| **Sort** | Sorts rows by a selected column in ascending or descending order. |
| **Focus** | Opens the table in a modal with the source visible and, when the source is editable, an **Apply** button. |

:::tip[Copy formats]
From the table header you can copy CSV for spreadsheets, Markdown for documentation, or a plain grid for quick notes.
:::

## Editing tables in curated pages

When you add a table to a curated page it becomes an editable table section. The section editor shows a spreadsheet-like grid on one side and a compact source panel on the other.

| Action | How it works |
|---|---|
| **Edit cells** | Click any cell to change its value. |
| **Add / remove rows** | Insert rows above or below the current selection, or delete selected rows. |
| **Add / remove columns** | Rename headers, insert columns, or remove columns that are no longer needed. |
| **Reorder columns** | Drag column headers to reorder the grid. |
| **Apply** | Save the edited table back to the curated page. |
| **Soft delete** | Remove the section; restore it before saving if you change your mind. |

:::tip[Large tables scroll, they do not paginate]
Tables in the curated-page editor and Preview tab scroll horizontally and vertically. They are not paginated, so long tables stay intact and searchable.
:::

## From table to curated page

The typical flow is:

1. Ask a Reflect question that requests a table, or open a mental model whose output is a table.
2. Inspect the rendered grid in the Preview tab.
3. Sort, search, or copy the table while you decide what to keep.
4. Copy the table (CSV, Markdown, or as a section) into a curated page.
5. In the curated page, refine cell values, add or remove rows, then save the page.

## Relationship to other focus pages

Tables often appear alongside narrative, diagram, and graph sections in the same envelope. A single Reflect result can contain a short narrative followed by a table that enumerates the details. You can mix all of these section types on one curated page.

- [Focus: narrative](./focus-narrative) for prose sections.
- [Focus: diagram](./focus-diagram) for visual flowchart sections.
- [Preview and curated pages](./preview-and-curated-pages) for the tab model this focus type fits into.

## Summary

The table focus turns Reflect output into editable grids. Previews give you copy, search, and sort controls; curated-page sections let you edit cells, rows, and columns live and save the result.
---

# Focus: graph
URL: https://architxtlabs.com/workspace/focus-graph
# Focus: graph

A **graph** directive asks architxt to explore the contextual graph itself: entities, edges, and the relationships that connect them. Unlike a diagram, which produces a static visual flowchart, a graph focus gives you an interactive network view that you can pan, zoom, filter, and inspect in the Preview tab.

## When to use a graph focus

Use a graph focus when you want:

- An interactive map of entities and their relationships.
- To explore neighbours, paths, or clusters rather than read a fixed visual.
- To start from one entity and discover what it connects to.
- Output that invites exploration before you settle on a static diagram or narrative.

## What a graph envelope looks like

A graph envelope contains one or more graph blocks. Each block has:

| Field | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **Name** | The title shown above the graph canvas. |
| **Nodes** | The entities rendered as interactive nodes. Each node shows its entity label and type. |
| **Edges** | The relationships between entities. Edge labels describe the relationship type or role. |
| **Details panel** | A side panel that opens when you select a node or edge. It shows properties, evidence, and attached mental models. |

Graph blocks are rendered inside an interactive canvas in the Preview tab. They are exploration-first views: you cannot directly edit the graph nodes and edges. The graph changes only when the underlying query or merged mental-model graph changes.

## Preview controls

Graph previews share the common envelope controls and add graph-specific exploration tools.

| Control | Behavior |
|---|---|
| **Zoom / Pan** | Scroll or pinch to zoom; drag the canvas to pan around the graph. |
| **Filter** | Hide nodes by type, edge label, or entity count to reduce visual noise. |
| **Search** | Jump to and highlight a node by name or entity type. |
| **Details** | Opens a panel with full properties and evidence for the selected node or edge. |
| **Focus** | Opens the graph in a modal where you can add its content to a curated page. Fit-to-page is enabled when the modal opens. |

## The Focus modal

The **Focus** modal is the main action surface for a graph. It opens the graph in a larger view and exposes controls for turning the graph into other section types.

| Action | Result |
|---|---|
| **Add diagram to page** | Converts the graph into a Mermaid diagram section on the active curated page. Evidence attached to nodes and edges is carried over to the diagram. |
| **Add table to page** | Converts the graph into a table section on the active curated page, giving you a structured view of nodes, edges, or both. |
| **Copy** | Copies the graph source or image, depending on the control you use. |
| **Fit to page** | The modal opens with fit-to-page enabled so the whole graph is visible at a glance. |

:::tip[Graphs become diagrams or tables, not editable graph sections]
A curated page cannot hold a live graph section. Instead, the Focus modal lets you add a **diagram** (static Mermaid flowchart) or a **table** derived from the graph. The graph itself stays read-only in the Preview tab.
:::

## From graph to curated page

The typical flow is:

1. Ask a Reflect question that requests a graph, or open a mental model whose output is a graph.
2. Inspect the interactive canvas in the Preview tab.
3. Pan, zoom, and filter until the important relationships are visible.
4. Select nodes to read their details and evidence.
5. Open the **Focus** modal and choose **Add diagram to page** or **Add table to page**.
6. In the curated page, edit the generated diagram source or table cells, then save the page.

## Relationship to other focus pages

Graphs and diagrams are closely related but serve different purposes. A graph is for exploration; a diagram is for presentation. Narrative and table sections can sit alongside either one, giving you prose context and structured data next to the visual.

- [Focus: narrative](./focus-narrative) for prose sections.
- [Focus: diagram](./focus-diagram) for static Mermaid flowcharts.
- [Focus: table](./focus-table) for structured grid sections.
- [Preview and curated pages](./preview-and-curated-pages) for the tab model this focus type fits into.

## Summary

The graph focus turns Reflect output into an interactive network canvas. Previews give you zoom, filter, search, and details controls; the Focus modal converts the graph into a diagram or table section on a curated page.
---

# Focus: evidence
URL: https://architxtlabs.com/workspace/focus-evidence
# Focus: evidence

Every **focus** result in the Workspace can carry **evidence**: the set of source memories, entities, or documents that justify the content. Evidence is not a separate focus type like narrative, diagram, table, or graph; it is the grounding layer behind all of them. When you know where a section came from, you can verify it, cite it, or dig deeper without guessing.

## What evidence is

Evidence is a list of references to source data. In practice this is usually Hindsight memory IDs that architxt used when generating or selecting the section. You can think of it as a bibliography entry for a paragraph, a table row, a diagram edge, or a graph node.

| Field | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **Memory IDs** | The stable identifiers of the Hindsight memories that support the section. |
| **Snippet** | A short excerpt from the source memory, when available, so you can see the context at a glance. |
| **Confidence** | Optional signal of how strongly the source memory supports the claim. |

Evidence is attached at the section level. A narrative may have one evidence list per heading; a table may have evidence per row or per block; a diagram carries evidence on its edges and nodes; a graph exposes evidence on selected nodes and edges in the Details panel.

## Where evidence appears

### Narrative

In a narrative preview, section-level actions include an evidence control. When invoked, it opens the **Evidence modal** and lists the memory IDs behind that section. If a section has no evidence, the control is disabled or hidden.

### Tables

Table blocks can carry evidence on the whole block or on individual rows. The Evidence modal shows the memory references that produced the columns and values you are reading.

### Diagrams

Diagram edges and nodes can carry evidence. When you add a graph-generated diagram to a curated page, the graph's edge evidence travels with it, so the diagram remains grounded in the same source memories.

### Graphs

Graph nodes and edges show evidence in the **Details** panel. Selecting a node or edge expands its properties and lists the source memories that established the relationship.

:::tip[Evidence is required for generated content]
Evidence arrays are required and preserved on narrative, diagram, and table envelope elements. This makes Reflect output verifiable by default.
:::

## The Evidence modal

The Evidence modal matches the focus-modal layout. It has a resizable panel that lists source memories, shows snippets, and lets you inspect the original context.

| Control | Behavior |
|---|---|
| **Source documents list** | Documents that contain one or more of the queried memories, with supporting-memory counts. |
| **Queried memories list** | The original memory IDs from the focus result, grouped by which documents and chunks they resolved to. |
| **Chunk detail** | The text of a selected chunk, with its chunk index and ID. |
| **Copy IDs** | Copies the memory IDs to the clipboard for use in queries or external citations. |
| **Resize** | Drag the modal footer or panel divider to make more room for long snippets. |

:::tip[Open evidence from any focus section]
If a section has evidence, the section-level actions include an evidence button. Use it to open the Evidence modal directly from the preview or curated-page editor.
:::

## Document metadata and real-world location

One of the main benefits of the Evidence modal is that it can point you back to the actual real-world document. When you select a document, the modal loads its metadata from Hindsight and shows:

| Field | What it means |
|---|---|
| **Title** | The human-readable document title, when available. |
| **Document ID** | The stable Hindsight document identifier. |
| **Hash** | A content hash that identifies the exact version of the document. |
| **Context** | The `context` field from the original `retain` call, often describing the source or purpose. |
| **Event date** | The date associated with the content, if one was supplied during retention. |
| **Created / Updated** | When the document was first retained and last updated. |
| **Tags** | Any tags attached to the document. |
| **Extra metadata** | Custom `document_metadata` fields supplied at retention time, such as a URL, file path, or ticket reference. |

If your retention pipeline stores a URL, file path, or ticket ID in `document_metadata`, that value appears here. This is how architxt bridges a generated answer back to the real-world document it came from.

## The two memory-ID hierarchies

The Evidence modal presents the same evidence through two complementary hierarchies.

### Documents → chunks → memory IDs

The **Source documents** panel starts with documents. For each document you see:

- How many of the queried memories were found in it.
- How many of those memories are flagged as supporting memories.
- The chunks inside that document that contain those memories.
- The individual memory IDs attached to each chunk.

This view is useful when you want to ask "which documents support this section?" and then drill into the exact chunk.

### Queried memories → documents → chunks

The **Queried memories** panel starts with the original memory IDs from the section. For each memory ID you see:

- The memory type, when known.
- Which documents the memory resolved to.
- Which chunks inside each document contain that memory.
- Any decomposed "world" memory IDs and their types.
- Observations that were skipped, if any.
- An unresolved error, if the memory could not be fetched.

This view is useful when you want to ask "where did this specific memory ID come from?" — for example, when a Reflect answer cites a memory that looks wrong.

:::tip[Two views of the same data]
Both panels resolve the same evidence payload. Use the documents-first view to browse by source document, and the memories-first view to debug a specific memory ID.
:::

## Chunk viewing and "Show in context"

A chunk is a slice of a Hindsight document that contains one or more supporting memories. Each chunk shows:

| Field | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **Chunk index** | The position of the chunk within the full document, so you can reason about ordering. |
| **Chunk ID** | The stable identifier for the chunk. |
| **Chunk text** | The actual text of the chunk, which you can read or copy. |
| **Supporting memory IDs** | The memory IDs found inside this chunk. |
| **Character count** | A quick indicator of chunk length. |

By default the right panel shows the selected chunk on its own. Toggle **Context** on a document to load all of its chunks and view the selected chunk inside the full document. In context mode:

- Chunks are sorted by chunk index.
- The selected chunk is highlighted and auto-scrolled into view.
- You can read the surrounding chunks to understand the original context.

:::tip[Render Markdown]
If a chunk contains Markdown formatting, enable the **Render** toggle to format it. Disable it to see the raw chunk text.
:::

## Recalling and viewing the document

The metadata panel tells you where the document lives, and the context view lets you read it. Together they let you:

1. Identify the real-world document from the title or `document_metadata`.
2. See which chunks contributed to the section.
3. Switch on **Context** to view the chunk inside the full retained document.
4. Copy the memory IDs or chunk text for follow-up queries or citations.

This is the main verification loop: generated content in the Workspace is traceable back to retained documents in Hindsight, and from there back to the real-world source.

## How evidence travels between sections

Evidence is preserved when one focus type is converted into another:

| Conversion | What happens to evidence |
|---|---|
| **Graph → Diagram** | Edge evidence from the graph is copied into the generated Mermaid diagram section. |
| **Graph → Table** | Graph-level evidence is copied into the node/edge table section. |
| **Reflect result → Curated page** | Each copied section keeps its own evidence list. |

This means a curated page assembled from multiple focus types remains fully traceable back to the original Hindsight memories.

## Why evidence matters

- **Verifiability** — Readers can inspect the source memories behind any claim.
- **Citations** — Memory IDs can be copied and referenced in follow-up queries.
- **Debugging** — If a Reflect answer looks wrong, check its evidence first to see what it was built from.
- **Trust** — Grounded answers in Reflect trace back to the documents and entities that produced them.

## From evidence to curated page

The typical flow is:

1. Run a Reflect query that produces narrative, table, diagram, or graph output.
2. Inspect each section and open the Evidence modal to see what supports it.
3. Copy the section into a curated page.
4. The curated page section retains its evidence list, so readers can verify it later.
5. If a section lacks evidence or the evidence looks wrong, refine the query or mental model and re-run Reflect.

## Relationship to other focus pages

Evidence underpins every focus type. The other pages describe the visible shape of the content; this page describes the invisible thread that ties that content back to source memories.

- [Focus: narrative](./focus-narrative)
- [Focus: diagram](./focus-diagram)
- [Focus: table](./focus-table)
- [Focus: graph](./focus-graph)
- [Preview and curated pages](./preview-and-curated-pages)

## Summary

Evidence is the set of source memory references behind every focus result. It appears in the Evidence modal for narratives, tables, diagrams, and graphs, and it is preserved when those sections are copied into curated pages. Keeping evidence intact makes Workspace output verifiable, citable, and trustworthy.
---

# Overview
URL: https://architxtlabs.com/context-patches/overview
# Overview

**Context Patches** is the part of architxt that builds and maintains a **contextual graph** on top of a Hindsight memory bank. It imports the bank's skeleton, discovers candidate nodes and edges, deploys contextual mental models, and keeps everything in sync through background jobs.

Think of it as the ongoing bridge between Hindsight's raw memory data and architxt's structured graph view. While Hindsight Sync moves documents, entities, mental models, directives, and settings between architxt and a bank, Context Patches keeps the graph itself alive: importing what Hindsight knows, proposing new candidates, deploying role-based models, and rerunning patches when config changes.

## What Context Patches does

When you open the **Context Patches** page and choose a server and bank, you can:

- Inspect the grounded **Graph** of entities and relationships already imported from Hindsight.
- Review **Candidates** — nodes and edges the system discovered but has not yet promoted into the graph.
- Manage **Mental Models** that are attached to graph nodes, edges, or seeds.
- Monitor and trigger **Sync Jobs** that run the import, deploy, and refresh pipeline.

## Page components

### Server and bank selectors

At the top of the page you choose the Hindsight **server** and **bank** you want to work with. Everything on the page — the graph, candidates, models, and jobs — is scoped to that server and bank.

### Config badges

Once a bank is selected, a row of badges describes how the bank is configured for contextual-graph operations:

| Badge | Meaning |
|---|---|
